title: AI Pays in Productivity but Trust Lags, TCS Study of 1,333 Executives Finds
excerpt: 84% of senior leaders in TCS's Enterprise AI Study rank productivity as AI's top benefit, but only 10% let AI agents act without human approval - and security and governance now outrank cost and speed in deployment decisions.
body:
• In TCS's Enterprise AI Study of 1,333 senior business and technology leaders across 25 countries, 84% ranked productivity improvement as the leading source of value from their AI investments.
  • Autonomy lags far behind adoption: only 10% of enterprises let AI agents execute decisions without human approval across multiple functions, and just 9% say their agents can securely orchestrate workflows across enterprise applications.
  • Security, risk and governance - ahead of cost and speed - is the top factor shaping where and how companies deploy AI, TCS found.
  • For Indian IT services firms and their global clients, the message is that the next phase of enterprise AI spending will be gated on guardrails, not on model capability.

Enterprises are getting measurable productivity out of artificial intelligence, but they are not yet willing to let it act on its own. That is the central finding of the TCS Enterprise AI Study: Intelligence that is Real, released by Tata Consultancy Services earlier this month and reported this week by SecurityBrief.

The study surveyed 1,333 senior business and technology leaders - C-suite executives, divisional leaders and senior vice presidents - across 25 countries and 12 industries, at organisations with annual revenues from US$500 million to more than US$20 billion. Eighty-four percent of the executives ranked productivity improvement as the leading source of value from AI investments, ahead of customer experience gains and new products and services. Only 10% said they had seen a revenue uplift.

The trust gap, in numbers

The autonomy figures are much thinner. Just 10% of global enterprises allow AI agents to execute decisions without human approval across multiple functions or business areas, and only 9% report AI agents capable of securely orchestrating workflows across enterprise applications. TCS found security, risk and governance is the number one factor shaping how and where AI is developed and deployed - ahead of cost, speed and ease of deployment.

Control questions run through the rest of the findings. Ninety percent of leaders said model independence matters in AI investment decisions, yet only 7% have an organisation-wide plan for switching providers. Thirty-four percent rated AI sovereignty requirements - control over data location, model choice and compliance - as a high or very high organisational risk, rising to 43% in Europe. And 39% are still assessing whether their AI initiatives generate enough value to justify their token and compute costs.

"Productivity is clearly where enterprises are seeing the greatest value from AI today. What seems to be holding organisations back - and rightly so - are concerns around security, governance, and resilience."

- Amit Kapur, Chief AI and Services Transformation Officer, TCS

Jobs, knowledge and the road ahead

On jobs, certainty is fading rather than hardening: the share of leaders saying it is too early to determine AI's effect on jobs rose from 4% in 2024 to 19% in 2026. Forty-four percent said important business knowledge still sits inside employees' heads or in fragmented documentation - a practical brake on automation - while 46% have deployed open-source AI for selected use cases. TCS frames the direction of travel as a "Human+AI operating model," in which AI moves from assisting employees towards taking on greater responsibility under enterprise controls.

For India's IT services industry, which sells AI transformation to exactly the executives surveyed, the study cuts both ways. Demand for AI work is real and productivity-led, but the buyers' own stated priorities - governance, model independence, sovereignty and provable value for compute spend - are now the terms on which contracts will be won. TCS's Kapur put the company's bet plainly: deploying AI responsibly, with the right guardrails and enterprise controls, will be the big focus of the next stage.
